glossary.definition: Making a call look as if a different agent made it. In the gallery a rogue agent holds a token whose signed act claim names the rogue, while the caller sends a header naming a trusted agent. The control reads the actor from the signed claim only and ignores the header.
A server accepts a token only if the aud claim names that server. A genuine token issued for another resource is refused, so tokens cannot be taken to a different service.

A trusted party is tricked into using its authority for someone else. In the gallery an MCP proxy with one static client ID at a third-party authorization server lets an attacker's dynamically registered client ride on the consent the user gave earlier.

A client registers itself with a server and receives its own client_id and redirect URI. Open registration lets anyone register a client, which is why the proxy must still ask the user for consent per client.

The authorization response carries an iss parameter naming the server that answered. The client compares it, as a simple string, with the issuer of the server it sent the request to, and stops on a mismatch.
A client that talks to more than one authorization server is steered to send a code meant for the good server to the evil one. The iss check on the authorization response is the named control.
Checking that the specific object requested (an account id, for example) belongs to the user in the token. A valid token with the right scope is not permission to read any object.

The resource parameter (RFC 8707) names the server a token is for, so the authorization server can restrict the token to it, usually through aud. The MCP authorization page requires clients to send it.

A hostile server supplies a metadata URL that points at an internal or link-local address, a name that resolves to loopback, or a redirect to a private range, hoping the client fetches it. The governed client refuses non-public targets. The gallery uses a fake network, so no real internal address is ever contacted.

An MCP server accepts a token not issued for it, or forwards the token it received to a downstream API. The MCP security page says servers MUST NOT accept tokens not explicitly issued for them. The control is to exchange the token for a separate one with its own audience.

wire.intro: Example data, nothing real. A token should work for one service only. Here is how that is enforced, and what goes wrong when a service skips the check.

steps.title: 1. The agent asks for a token for one named service

token.label: The token that came back (for the mail API only)

header.name: alg
header.note: How the signature was made. The receiver checks it with the issuer's public key.

header.name: kid
header.note: Which of the issuer's keys to check the signature with.

claims.name: iss
claims.note: Who issued this token. Receivers only trust issuers they know.

claims.name: sub
claims.note: Who the token is about: the person.

claims.name: aud
claims.note: Who this token is FOR. It was minted for the mail API because the request named resource=https://mail.example.com.

claims.name: exp
claims.note: When it stops working (a Unix time).

steps.notice: The resource parameter makes the auth server stamp the service's address into aud. The token is born knowing who it is for.

jargon.meaning: A request parameter naming the service the token will be used at (a resource indicator).
The one service a token is meant for. A service should refuse a token whose aud is not itself.
A pass that works for whoever holds it, like a cinema ticket. Anyone who copies it can use it.

steps.title: 2. The agent tries the same token at a different service

headers: Authorization: Bearer [the mail token from step 1]
error_description="aud does not include this API"

steps.notice: The calendar API reads aud, sees mail.example.com, and refuses. A buggy or hijacked agent cannot spend a token somewhere it was not meant for.

jargon.meaning: The server refuses because it does not accept the credentials presented.

steps.title: 3. The bug: a service that does not check aud

headers: Authorization: Bearer [the mail token from step 1]

steps.notice: This service only checks the signature, so any genuine token from this auth server gets in. That is token passthrough: the service becomes a confused deputy that accepts tokens meant for others.

jargon.meaning: Accepting or forwarding a token that was not issued for you.
A trusted service tricked into using its authority for someone who should not have it.
